review_text:
I'm coming from a 1440p 60hz monitor so adjusting back down to 1080p is going to take some time. But even with the lower resolution (which I can clearly tell, sadly) I'm very happy with this monitor. I currently don't have a GPU that can push 1440p 144hz and I probably won't for a while so I wanted to try a 1080p 144hz for the time-being. I only have a gtx 1060 and running dual monitors i can't even push 144hz on most of the games I play.

The last 144hz monitor I tried was the HP Omen 25" '144hz' monitor and it was an awful experience. The backlight bleed was horrendous.. the color was terrible.. the backlight was not uniform with the left, middle, and right side.. the only good thing about that monitor was the superb build quality. I just don't understand how that monitor has good ratings. Maybe it's just TN trash.. I don't know.

I'm not sure if I got super lucky or what but there are 0 dead pixels, 0 backlight bleed showing at all.. this is the first monitor I've ever owned out of 2~ dozen that is just completely black when on.. without any sort of bleeding light.

The curve is definitely noticeable, but it doesn't bother me.. and I think this is probably a huge personal preference where it might irritate some people. Luckily, I'm easily able to adapt.

If MSI had a 1440p 144hz 24" version of this monitor.. I think I would gift this, MAG24C, to a friend and buy that.. because personally I think 1440p on a 24" is perfect... or 4k on a 27"+... I think 1080p is good on 22" or lower.. 1080p quality just doesn't look good on a 24" in my eyes. That said, this monitor is really nice.... so I'm going to adjust.

The only thing I need to test more/try and notice is ghosting. I mostly play games like overwatch, hearthstone, fortnite, dead by daylight (perfect monitor for this darkish game) and single player titles like the witcher/tomb raider.

I might have to try the Optix MAG27CQ.. owning the MAG24C gives me a lot of confidence in this brand/model line-up.

Edit: after using for a day, I have noticed that the brightness does shift depending on vertical and horizontal orientation. It's not bad, but noticeable coming from IPS.

Update 10/2/2018: removing 1 star because the vesa mounting should have had a better solution. MSI should have included adapters with this monitor to make the vesa mounting usable. (one thing I liked about the HP omen 25" was they included a very nice vesa adapter) If vesa is deal-breaker for you I would STAY AWAY from this monitor. It might work for you, it might not... again.. monitors like this should 100% include a vesa adapter to help with mounting.

UPDATE 11/26/2018: removing 1 star because I started to notice a buzzing sound during the night. I couldn't figure out where it was coming from, but then I noticed that it corresponded to the BLUE LED on the front when the monitor was in 'sleep mode.' I tried to look in the OSD for an option to disable this light completely, but there isn't an option for that. This is a pretty annoying buzz I have to deal with during the night (I could just turn the monitor off, but it's 2018.. there should be an option to disable it in the settings). I really hope there is a firmware update that can resolve this issue. I still think this is a great 1080p 144hz display, but definitely some quirks one has to deal with (vesa is awkward and will not work with some vesa solutions. Buzz coming from blue LED with no option to disable/turn-off) The buzz is not noticeable during regular usage.
title: extremely surprised by this monitor... my last 144hz was trash (hp omen 25")

review_text:
Pros:
1) perfect fit for IPAD 3 (new IPAD),
2) solid impact protection,
3) not too bulky and
4) nice quality feeling materials.

Cons:
1) The front cover blocks the camera lens when it is attached to the back of the ipad, which is the most common and convenient place to keep it when using the ipad's main camera,
2) on the sides (by the power button and opposite), the butyl rubber surround often folds over and slips off the side of the ipad when handling normally. It's easily put back in place but is just annoying. and
3) Pricey, even without considering cons 1 and 2 above.

The missing hole for the camera lens and the butyl material by the power button reduced my 5 star rating to 3 stars....it's that annoying. I may even drill out the camera lens hole myself.

I've used this product for 5 months now. Other cases I considered were: a. Griffin Survivor, b. GumDrop and c. the Otterbox Defender. Of these, only the Seido and Gumdrop seemed to present a realistic balance between protection and value. The Defender and Survivor were just way over the top in terms of cost and construction. (All of this stuff seems to be injection molded.) Admittedly however, if cost were of no consideration I probably would have bought the military influenced Survivor.

Ipad protectors are all hugely overpriced for what they are made of! With the Seido's glaring flaws, I seriously consider other alternatives before parting with my credit card number. Also, I would have bought an Apple branded case but none of them seemed to protect well against drops on the corners, especially in the kitchen or garage where the surfaces are very hard.

The Seido Active Case product came with the following parts:

a) The "shock absorber" a butyl rubber membrane that fits around the sides and back of the ipad,

b) The "back cover" a hard plastic shell that fits over and locks the butyl rubber surround onto the sides and back of the ipad, protecting the back and corners and

c) The "front cover" A hard plastic shell which clips over the front of the ipad to protect the screen when the ipad is not in use. It can be clipped on the back of the ipad for convenient storage when walking around while using the ipad or can be used as a multi position stand to watch the ipad hands free. When in use, your fingers touch the actual ipad screen unless you buy a separate film type face protector.) I like that and did not want a transparent film screen cover for the same reason some people do not like condoms. It's been 5 months now and I am very happy with that decision.
title: good protection but 2 notable flaws

review_text:
Not sure if others have had issues with htis or not, but my lens would cause severe smearing/blur/shake hand held at any f-stop above f-4. From F- 4.5 up, all shots below say 1/30 of a second showed severe shake blur- I was gettign better shots without IS below 1/3 of a second- even handhhnadholding this lens with no IS at 2 seconds, the photos had less shake blur than when hte IS was on- this happened every time I tested shooting both ways- I tried it on another camera, and same issue- wide open, the IS worked flawlessly. I suspected soemthign was wrogn hte first day I got the lens, and thought "I was gettign way slower photos than that without any blur with my cheapo kit lens 18-135 IS, why is there such a blur at 1/20 second with this lens?" I then tested it out hte next day, and usre enough, the IS was actually causing blur hand held. I was very dissappointed as I really wanted this lens to replace my kit lens 18-135. I will say however that the shots I got with the lens with high shutter speeds looked very good with great contrast and color compared to my old 18-135 IS. The feel of the lens was solid and comfortable unlike the 18-135 IS which just felt cheap and plastic. The 24-105 was also very smooth action and a real pleasure to use compared to the 18-135 IS. Coupled with the Canon 1DX it was making soem very fine photos- I just wished my particular 24-105 didn't have the defective IS as I was really really wantign to use it with my new Canon 1DX for soem truly superb photos. What few photos I did get with hte combo looked really nice- so that's why I gave the review 4 stars- the lens IQ was fantastic compared to my old 18-135 IS, but mechanically, I just got a defective unit sadly- which I had to pay shipping back to the seller, but thankfully it was only around $10 with insurance applied- but still- I'd rather be shootign this lens daily instead of havign to wait for the refund swo I can go out and find one and try before buying (I'll know right away if ones I try do the same IS shake/blur thing- it's that obvious when hte IS is defective- wish I knew how to upload a photo to show how bad the shake blur was- but basically, you literally could not tell what an item was- it was that bad- Shots of text, there was no way you could read it- it was all a severe blur/shake- and always in a diagonal direction too-top left to bottom right - all three issues were present-

Overall, the sharpness,clarity,color,contrast with htis lens was fantastic- The versatility is pretty good too, although I will miss the 18-136 range of my old kit lens, which seemed almost perfect range (around 150 or therabouts for the long end would be really good in my opinion), and liek I said, the build quality was really nice too- it also had full time manual override for the focusing which is really nice too for those times when you try to focus on a bird or deer or soemthign near brush, and the lens can't lock onto subject- fumbling for the manual switch often makes you lose focus altogether- but haviing full time manual override means you can keep focus o nthe subject while focussing the manual focus ring- The weight was good for me too- It woudl probably be a bit heavy for some, but I liek the weight just fine- but of course I lug around the Sigma Bigma all day too, so the 24-105 felt liek a featherweight to me-

review_text:
Same day update..

I checked the cables again, but this time with the power on my phone down to 40%.. and found that the 3 foot cable was now reading 1.86 amps.. Still way shy of the 3 amps advertised.. The 6 foot cable was giving me 1.38 amps, and the 10 foot was still at 1.09 amps.. But upon doing a little more testing, the end of one of the cables came off.. That part that you are supposed to grab, that is metal, to hold to plug and unplug the cord.. It literally just fell right off.. I took a picture so you can see what I mean.. They are lucky that I am leaving it at 2 stars at this point..

Original, but just earlier in the day review..

They were cheap.. But in my point, not cheap enough..

I have a tester here to test the amps going through, and the voltage.. What I got when testing it off of my N200 phone with a 56% charge and off of a 2 amp wall charger was this.. The 3 foot cable, I got 1.38 amps at 5 volts.. The 10 foot cable I got 1.09 amps at 5 volts.. No where near the 3 amps that they advertise. In comparison, I bought 3 different auctions, with 3 different cords.. My next cord that I checked with the same specs, I got 2.10 amps out of the 3 foot cord.. and the cord that I have been using got 1.99 amps out of that 3 foot cord.. So basically, there is no way it could have been my phone or the wall outlet that was limiting if from not at least reaching the 2 amps that the wall adapter was capable of.

The bad part is, the cord that I did get 2.1 amps off of, was only $2 more for the same size and number of cords.. The other thing that I did not like was.. The ones that were not much more.. Those were more flexible, and also came with a nice rubber piece to hold things together.. I like that they gave the rubber piece instead of just a standard twist tie.. These cords are about two to three times as stiff as any other decent cord that I have used.. I do not know why they are so stiff.. Maybe they will loosen up with time??

If I bought these for something that did not have a fast charging rate, or maybe did not use a lot of power, like say, charging my automatic soap dispenser, then not having 3 amp charging is not going to make any difference.. and that is what I will probably use them for..

One thing I did notice when trying to use them.. They go into the USB C end mostly all the way with a decent stiffness.. But then they just stop about 1/8" from all the way in.. You need to give them a little extra push to get them to go in all the way.. I tried multiple lengths of cords out of this pack, and they all do that.. It is nice that they are that stiff because it helps them stay in better.. and I am sure that will loosen up with time too..

In the end, they are cheap.. But no decent tie on them, cords are too stiff, and advertising them as 3 amps when they are more like an 1.5 amp.. and with better cords only being about $2 more for 5 cords, or $0.40 more per cord, these are clearly lacking.. Which is why I only gave them a 2 star rating.. But I could not go with 1 star because they do work, and I have had cheaper and worse cords in the past.. So that is the bump up to 2 stars..
title: stiff, and more like 1.5 amp cords.. Not 3 amp

review_text:
If you return to your car one evening, only to find that your car stereo has been stolen, now you know where it went! Just kidding, but I do wonder exactly where these came from.

This is a unique little item that I do not quite understand the concept for, but the results most certainly can't be argued with. According to the manufacturer the product consists of car stereos that are pulled from brand new Volkswagon cars. This story does not make a lot of sense though. Wouldn't it just be easier and cheaper to buy these before they are installed in the cars and have to be pulled out? I'm sure that there is some kind of wacky story behind this product, but the manufacturer really does not elaborate.

The entire unit is mounted in the center of what seems to be a single, very heavy duty speaker enclosure. There does not seem to be any separation between the two built-in speakers (to the left and right of the console) or between the speakers and the console. There could possibly be some sort of "wall" to isolate the parts inside the enclosure, but it doesn't look like it.

The very heavy duty (and heavy!) speaker enclosure gives the device some great range and bass response. The sound is very full and rich. There is not a lot of separation between the speakers so discerning between the left and right channels in stereo recordings can be a bit difficult. The two front firing speakers do not lend themselves well to stereo reproduction. Then again, a car (which this device was designed to operate in) does not make for a great environment for reproducing stereo sound either.

The device has the appearance of an old style boom box, but is not portable in any way. Even if it had batteries, lifting and lugging it around would be quite a chore. The unit works best if set in the middle of a room with decent acoustics. A wooden entertainment center would be ideal for using with this device.

The remote that comes with the device is about the size of my thumb. Because it was designed to be used inside of a vehicle that range is extremely limited and spotty. The IR transmitter has a range of about 10 feet, which has to be line-of-sight. I would have to say that it comes pretty close to being entirely useless unless you are standing directly in front of the thing, which kind of defeats the entire purpose of using a "remote".

The device has plenty of input options and has all of the latest bells and whistles that you would expect from a car stereo, other than the ability to do video playback and control accessories. For simply listening to music it works wonderfully though. I would say that the price is a little on the high side for a product containing "salvaged" parts, but I also believe that most people hearing it will feel that they are definitely getting their money's worth.
title: Who Took My Car Stereo?

review_text:
I've had these headphones since September of 2019, but I didn't use them often until recently. I was wearing them the other day and one earbud popped out and dropped into very muddy water. It took me a couple minutes to find it, and once I did, I rinsed the mud off with clean water. I thought they only had a water resistant rating and therefore expected the earbud to die. Nope. It kept working. That was when I checked and saw they had an IPX8 rating (waterproof).

Waterproofing aside, I find the battery life sufficient for whatever I am doing. These can outlast me working in the yard and I am yet to put the advertised 6 hour runtime to the test. I like that the case can charge the earbuds, though I never really need that feature.

I mostly listen to mostly audio books, but the sound is quite good. The bass is highly improved if you can get the earbuds seated in your ear just right, though movement tends to make them shift a bit.

Then there's the range. I never really need to go to far from my phone, but I can if I need to... One day I didn't realize I left my phone in the kitchen until I was out of my house and the audio started getting choppy. I reached to my pocket to check my phone and realized I left it in the house. The distance was impressive.

The last feature I can think of is the phone call quality. I was on a call this morning and we both had HD audio phones so the sound was incredible. It was like being in the same room together. I didn't ask the other person how I sounded, but they never asked me to repeat something.

Taking into consideration the price of these headphones, I am more than pleased with them. I am not saying they are merely acceptable because of the low price. These sound and perform much better than I expected.

review_text:
Not sure how there are so many people who like it so much. I'm giving it 3 stars because it functions as intended. The bluetooth is easy to program, and it's stable on my Galaxy S8. Unfortunately, the volume on it isn't that great. The OTA radio stations are much louder. There is a way on the device to make it louder (the so called volume knob), but note that if you take it to 30 (max volume), it will be peaking quite heavily, so much of the audio may sound extremely distorted. I ended up leaving it somewhere between 20 and 25 for maximum fidelity. Not like there is much of it. It's an FM transmitter. No matter how fancy of equipment you have, it'll sound pretty crummy compared to a hardwired solution.

When I set it, I originally set it to the high 80s MHz. There was a huge issue, though. It's not stable at those frequencies. I have a couple stations I would listen to normally (90.9, 92.1), and no matter where the frequency is between 87.5 and 93MHz, it would add much static to the stations. Up high at the 107-108 area, it was fine. Unfortunately, there are still quite a few stations up north, so but I was happily able to find an empty spot that seems to work.

The plug fits into the 12v socket very solidly. Nice and tight. But it's not perfect. If it tough it the wrong way, it'll lose power, and I'd have to wait for it to boot up and my phone to pair with it again. In other words, the next/previous buttons on there are pretty useless. There's also no on-off switch, which is a bummer.

The microphone picks up a lot of road noise, which really drowns out my voice. At full volume, I can barely hear the other end during a phone call.

Ultimately, I don't like this product. If it wasn't so cheap, I'd just return it. But alas, it functions as a hands-free bluetooth device. And I will only use it for a month or two until I get a proper head unit for it before I retire this sucker. For a couple months' worth of usage so I won't get a cell phone ticket, the price is justified.
title: It functions, but it's not at all a great product like many people make it out to be

review_text:
This router can't simultaneously use WPA2 encryption with a WDS bridge. The ASUS website says as much if you dig a little.

In order to use WDS, you have to either use antiquated encryption (WES) which is known to have security flaws, or you must use *no encryption at all*. Neither option is in any way acceptable. Both WPA2 and WDS are at least 15 year old standards. Common encryption standards with WDS should be a given.

I'm returning both routers that I bought. It's a shame, too, because the router looked like it had a very user-friendly front-end.
title: Router Doesn't Support WPA2 Encryption with WDS!!

When I get back I plug in the Trips and Pics and use the software to save the data in the Trips and Pics format and then again in GPX format. I then copy the GPX format file to the CF card from my camera.

My camera is a Canon 40D and I shoot in RAW. I use Downloader Pro to rename the RAW files and integrate the GPS data as well as convert a copy to DNG. That process works great and I now have GPS data included in both the CR2 sidecar file and the converted DNG file. When I use Lightroom 2 to export to JPEG the GPS data in in the JPEG file also.

I'll get a different GPS dohicky someday (or a camera that includes GPS) that saves the above steps but for now I am very pleased with the Trips and Pics and would recommend it to anyone in the same situation.

I have not used the included software to add GPS data to JPEG files or much else other than converting the Trips and Pics format data to GPX. It works great for that.

Kept my idle temps for 2 x GTX 680 FTW+ in SLI around 30C and at 10 minutes of heavy sim racing load at just under 59C. I'm using 2 Corsair H55s and a Cool Master HAF X case.

The installation of the bracket and cooler took about 25 minutes for the first one and 20 minutes for the second one. It actually took quite a lot of time to rewire everything and position the radiators and fans in the case (one hour plus).

The results are significantly cooler than the stock cooler, but depending on your radiator placement and case, it could end up heating up the room more. The was the only solution for SLI that I looked at (outside of custom watercooling) that could fit 2 coolers in my case for SLI. The brackets make the card a little unstable against the motherboard, compared to the stock cooler.

All in all, I'm happy with the results. I would suggest getting a cooler with longer hoses than the H55 (which are the cheapest on the market refurbished at $50 each). It would actually be fairly easy to put the GTX680s back in their stock case/cooler to sell them and use this bracket system with another card if necessary.

A 10 inch tablet is too big for the keyboard to use effectively, even with large hands, as holding the tablet on each end doesn't allow my thumbs to reach the middle keys.  By the way, it's difficult to hold with one hand being large but also very thin.  Although the display appears sharp most of the time, you can pick up the fact that the lower dpi from the 8" version makes a noticeable difference.  Go smaller.  Pictures taken with this tablet don't look very good on the 10" display but look better when downloaded to my desktop computer, however, my 2 year old phone takes better pics.  You'll need to jump through a bunch of hoops to get access to Google stuff, if you want it.  You will be getting stuck with tons of unused apps that you'll never get rid of.  Almost 7 gigs worth.  There's no GPS so unless you have an external BT GPS receiver and some sort of network access for maps then you're lost.  Places where you get position and maps you don't really need it.  Even with a lower dpi rating than the 8", watching movies or other video from amazon prime looks pretty good.  Battery life is very good and network access is excellent - connects and stays connected.  I installed a Unicorn Beetle case that has a built in screen protector that makes holding and using this tablet somewhat easier.  Also, using a B16 keyboard helps if you can get used to it - keys are at both ends at the bottom of the display.  Nice to have the SD card slot.  If it was my choice I would go smaller, 8-9" display, something with GPS, something with less ads (if that's possible these days).  They do make it easy to shop Amazon, though.

I've received a one time authorization from Onkyo to have my system repaired under warranty. I'm going to raise my star count to 2 because of they said they will cover it, however, I dropped the unit off at an authorized repair center on 4/18/13. I check in every Friday to get a status. As a result of having to wait so long and based upon the reports that others have waited so long - I dug deep and went and bought the Yahmaha 3020. It's absolutely awesome. Amazing separation and sound quality. Did not have to adjust the volume once to hear the dialogue during the entire movie. Something I've never had with the Onkyo. review_text:
This is a review of the Samsung Galaxy J7 Perx for the Boost Mobile prepaid network. Note this phone is locked to Boost Mobile, there are other versions of the same phone which will be locked to other providers. Do NOT purchase this phone other than for the Boost Mobile network.

My Galaxy J7 Perx is replacing a Samsung Galaxy 5. It has a larger screen, and a longer run time. There is a lot of bloat / spy ware included with the phone (Facebook as an example can't be uninstalled). Google spying just comes with Android, it's built in. There is a fair bit of other junk Boost Mobile included (Instagram and other stuff) which can't be removed, some of it (but not all of it) can be disabled.

Many complain the phone is slow. If your phone is slow the cause may be a defective phone OR bloatware. Facebook for example must scan all your gmail messages and phone home, this can take both time and resources. Other products will behave similarly, during the initial "scan" of your device by the bundled applications the phone may be a bit sluggish. After a while, either by stopping bloat, or letting it run through your stuff, the phone should be relatively snappy.

The phone is fast for me, faster than a Galaxy 5 or 6, not as good of course as a Galaxy 8. While it has 8 cores, and can issue 2 instructions (sometimes) per cycle on a 2.3 GHz clock the 8 instruction pipeline doesn't function out of sequence. Thus each instruction must be processed in order. The GPU is fairly powerful, this phone has a 5.5" screen and may not quite be a phablet phone. It offers 720 x 1200 resolution (not 1080 x 1920). While this is considered HD, it is the lower HD standard, most often used by broadcasters. If you get close to the screen, some pixelation is visible.

It has a long run time. On Boost mobile this phone had 5 bars of 4G LTE while my older Galaxy 5 using the same Sprint network via Freedompop had only 2 bars. Download speed for this phone is almost 3 times as fast as the speed for my Galaxy 5 after trying several different locations. It may be due to improved phone technology, or due to Boost Mobile getting better data access than Freedompop, but it is nice to have decent speed.

I would have preferred a 7 or 8 inch phone, literally a tablet phone, but my budget didn't permit it. My Boost Mobile plan does have tethering (hotspot) and speeds were about half on the hotspot what they were directly to the phone. So hotspot isn't as fast as a direct 4G connection. My speed on this phone averages about 30 Mbs download and a bit under 9Mbs upload.

The play store works well. No fingerprint scanner, for security use a PIN. :(

Considering the world we live in, where Facebook, Google and whatever else mines our personal information and adversely affects device performance, this is a decent reasonably low cost phone. The Galaxy J7 Perx goes on sale sometimes for as low as $90, in my case the plan I wanted from Boost Mobile was expiring soon and this caused me to pay $129 per phone, which is still not that bad.

The front camera is 8 megapixels and works better in low light than other cameras I've used, a slightly lower resolution camera with better low light capability and less blur is an advantage to a few extra megapixels in my opinion. Play store, Google calendar and what not work well. Samsung by default sticks its browser in the quick launch tab. You will notice a cluster of Google, Samsung and Boost Mobile apps many of which provide similar or identical function. If you want Chrome, just move the Samsung browser out and Chrome in. Chrome is better.
title: Decent and fast budget phone, good less blur and decent low light 8 MP camera, Android 7 and tons of bloatware. :)

review_text: I need to rant.  I purchased this item on November 2022, and have not had occasion to use it very much since that time.  Today, I decided I needed to brush up on it, to find my way somewhere unfamiliar.  I am not a tech genius, who automatically, intuitively, just somehow KNOWS how to operate every new electronic device I pick up.  (Nor do I have access to a printer.)  So I went digging for my USER’S MANUAL to figure out what I needed to do - that I was SURE MUST have been in the box with the NEW GPS.  Could not find it anywhere.  So I contacted Garmin online to ask them to send me a printed User’s Manual, thinking that I had obviously misplaced mine that “must have come with it in the box”.  But I was told that Garmin no longer provides a printed User’s Manual with their products - AT ALL.  Not even upon request.  They simply won’t provide one.  You must go find it online and print it out for yourself, if you want one.  We’re not talking about a just couple of pages.  Now, these must be people who have never experienced a prolonged power outage, or who assume that one ALWAYS has access to a printer, or a computer while on-the-go in an unfamiliar place, to have to go searching for a USER’S MANUAL on some stranger’s computer in a pinch, or on the road, lost somewhere, no access to a computer, car broken down, dead battery…any number of scenarios where one would LOVE to have a PRINTED hardcopy.  Wouldn’t a PRINTED User’s Manual be an obvious necessity for ANY unfamiliar new electronic device?  ESPECIALLY a product intended for travel use away from home?  The most BASIC assistance one might expect, to come WITH a brand new product purchased in its original box??  Their customer service on their website was less than helpful, and refused to send me a printed Owner’s Manual.  It’s up to me to get one - on my own.  I am honestly outraged by this lack of service.  It may be a great product; but what good is it, if you can’t figure out how to USE IT, just from some inborn psychic ability?  Can you tell I’m not pleased with their lack of service?  Now, I am not a stranger to electronic devices; I learned to use them as they were in their infancy, just coming onto the business scene; but I wasn’t born with a smart phone in my hands, either. review_text:
I bought this keyboard based on all the positive reviews. Replacing my corded Apple keyboard was not really necessary, but I decided to go all wireless. I love the way both my Logitech Performance MX mouse and the keyboard use the same receiver (hint: you can insert the receiver in a USB cable, connect to your USB hub, and clip the business end to something near the top of your desk if you're concerned about signal strength).

Compared with my old Apple corded keyboard (vintage 2009), the Logitech build and design quality is equal, at best. Compared to the 2013 Apple corded keyboard the Logitech is better. That is not to say it's a thing of beauty. The industrial designers couldn't decide on a corner radius for all keys, so some have an ugly rounded corner. The Caps Lock key is hideous, plus there is no indication as to whether caps lock is on or off.

The designers also couldn't decide whether to make the key tops convex or concave, so the F keys are the former most other keys are the latter. Except the bottom row. Huh??? One more jab: the key labels are ugly / awkward on keys that share two characters. Apple keyboards are superior in that respect. (…and some people can't understand how Apple's obsession with design truly does make for a better user experience).

Connectivity and setup are very good. The action is as good as or better than my best old Apple keyboard.

Even a small amount of light seems to be plenty to power the keyboard.

Finally, I ordered the white and silver model and wish I had gotten the black and silver one.

UPDATE OCT. 2017: Okay, so about three years after owning this keyboard, it stopped working without warning. After digging around online, I discovered that the internal rechargeable battery had probably died. But get this – Logitech swears the battery is not replaceable. Wrong! They lie!!

You need to finesse the battery drawer open, using a tiny jeweler's screwdriver and tapping out the drawer gently with a small hammer (not using the hunting knife and mangling the keyboard like the guy on YouTube). Then you order the new Maxell ML2032 battery from eBay for $4.00. Sorry Logitech, I won't be buying a new keyboard from you after all. This confirms my opinion that Logitech makes very good physical products but then you get mediocre customer service, horrible user interface, and bad misinformation. BOO!!! Oh, and don't get me started on their cheesy, unresponsive Logitech Options system preference (Mac).
title: Four stars (but read the update!)

Because this monitor is aimed at gamers, I'd like to first share that I am not a super competitive gamer. That being said, I do enjoy playing some online first person shooters. I tried this monitor on the basis that I was interested in how big a difference the higher refresh rate would make.

I know this isn't going to be a popular opinion, but honestly, it doesn't make as big a difference as I thought it would given the hype I read. Is it technically better and can it give very talented players an advantage? Yes, for sure. However, as more of a casual gamer, I find that I enjoy higher resolution more than higher refresh rate (above 60hz). And yes, my rig is capable of playing new games at 1080p at around 144 FPS (though at times dips to closer to 100).

The thing that really makes this monitor unusable to me is the PPI. A 27 inch+ monitor with 1080p resolution for anything but gaming just looks like garbage. Text looks so bad that it almost hurts my eyes to read on it. Pictures look bad. Video looks bad. The color reproduction on this isn't all that great either.

I guess what I am trying to say is.. unless you are a super competitive gamer that only uses their computer to play games, and you are a huge Samsung fan, then I would not recommend this monitor. Luckily, I am able to return it.

review_text:
What I was looking for was a decent monitor with 'good blacks' and 'clear text' even when the brightness & contrast are turned up. I like a relatively bright screen, but I want my black background to look like the monitor is turned off. I use Photoshop for solely for fixing up photos of my kids, so I'm not professional. I causally play FPS games once an a while, but I'm not hard-core. I mostly use my machine for coding, word documents, etc.

I had the following monitors hooked up all at once: an Acer K242HL-LED, an ASUS VN247H-P and the View Sonic VX2452MH. They are all the same price range give-or-take a fist full of dollars.

The Acer was terrible. The 'blacks' were mostly gray and the text looked terrible. The ASUS was much better than the Acer, but it was hard to get good blacks and good contrast. I spent some time messing around with the settings but never had a satisfactory configuration.

I was about to write how bad the ghosting is and was surprised it was so bad on a 2ms monitor -- particularly bad when you drag a window around with dark text on a blue-ish background (think Office 2003/SSMS). Then I remembered seeing an option for "Response Time" in the settings. I just changed it from the default of "Ultra Fast" to "Standard" and there is no ghosting at all.

The ViewSonic is not as nice as the previous version (which I've paired this one with). The buttons for the OSD are physical buttons where as the previous version used a touch-sensitive bevel.

The ViewSonic is by far the winner of these three and is a good buy once you've configured it correctly.
title: 3-Way comparison of Sub-$200 monitors

Was attempting to use this with a Clearstream 2V antenna. After several hours of troubleshooting and talking to Winegard Tech Support, it seems the pre-amp is bad. I got no signal through whatsoever and even tried multiple connecting cables. Installation was easy enough but receiving a product DOA deserves zero stars if it were possible.

Update: After writing my initial review I spoke to a product support expert at Winegard. She felt the problem may be that the pre-amp is sending to much power to the TV which can cause complete loss of signal. Found this hard to believe but that was what she said. In trying to troubleshoot the product, I unplugged the power inserter module thinking that the normal signal (un-amplified signal) would simply pass through the pre-amp. I was looking to test each component individually to determine where the problem was. I also did not receive any signal at all doing this. She said the pre-amp circuitry needs power. So an un-amplified signal will not simply pass through the component. Just FYI in case anyone else is having difficulty and trying to find the problem.

So while this device may not have been DOA as previously thought, it clearly did not work at all for me.

It is unfortunate that the reviews for the DVI-D to VGA (24 + 1 pin) and DVI-I to VGA (24 + 5 pin) are combined for this brand and type of product. The 24 + 1 pin configuration almost never works. Only a few specific setups allow VGA signal over DVI-D links. The 4 additional pins in the 24 + 5 pin design are the ones that carry the analog signal that allow the use of a VGA monitor with a DVI connector. If your video card only has a DVI-D connector, it is likely that you will not be able to connect to an old VGA monitor. That is not a limitation of this adapter, but of your video card.

Note that these adapters are for the output side only. You cannot connect this adapter to the DVI input on your monitor and get signal from a VGA output on your computer.

review_text: We basically got this to restrict my 7-year-olds usage on his iPad, Mac, and Roku because I was tired of policing every single thing separately.  First off, it connected well, no issues there.  The app you put on your phone is pretty user friendly, however, it was restricting things that we didn't have checked.  For instance, our 18-year-old was put under "Adult" and it wouldn't let her update any apps or visit certain benign websites.  So we switched her to "None" and she was still having issues updating apps on her phone and constantly complained that the internet on her PC was slow.  My son's Roku stopped working several times and wouldn't let him watch certain videos without throwing up a "you need a Google account to watch this" warning.  So, we monkeyed with the settings in the app and finally got that to work but we had to set it to where NO restrictions were set in order for him to get past the warning.  Defeats the whole purpose of this thing.  Lastly, it slowed our internet and eventually crashed it.  We unhooked it and had to reset EVERYTHING that was hooked up through it.  I factory reset the thing and put in back in the box to be returned.  Apple has parental controls on their stuff so we're using those for now.  I'm glad this works for some people but it's not great and I wouldn't recommend it.  If your kids are smart like mine, they'll figure out that you can switch to cellular data on phones/tablets as a go-around.  If you also have different wi-fi channels set up, they'll figure out that this only connects to one of them and they can switch to the other one as yet another go-around.  So, it's not foolproof.  My advice: use what's there on your devices and cellular service and save yourself almost a hundred bucks.  It's probably better than the service you'll get with the circle.
title: Waste of Money

review_text:
ATTENTION STOMACH SLEEPERS... You found them!

I have been on the lookout for "sleep headphones" that I could tolerate for years. I tried some typical earbuds but they pressed into my ear when I lay on my side. I tried the headband kind but they were hot. I settled on the flat headphones, the ones that are disc-shaped and cost about $10. Well, that's about all they're worth because they fall apart in a couple of months as I stomach-slept on them.

I was skeptical and worried that these would hurt when I laid on my head/ear down on the pillow. It turns out they are tiny and you can do it with only a tiny bit of discomfort that I'm sure I'll get used to.

You have the choice of six "soothing sounds" you can load onto them with the 1More app (it has a small library to choose from but the buds themselves can hold six at a time) or use your phone and connect via Bluetooth. They don't have a microphone, no calls. Some of the soothing sounds aren't very good but there's a handful that would work for me.

Yes, did you catch that, you can use these like regular Bluetooth earbuds and play podcasts, music, anything on your phone. Now, music doesn't come across and rich and clear as it does with my Galaxy Buds Pro (as an example). My Galaxy Buds Pro are 3x the size of these. It's good enough for sleeping. For spoken word, I can't tell the difference between my wired earphones and the 1More earbuds.

There are already photos of the buds so I'll just toss in two of my head. Keep in mind I have a large head - like can't-wear-baseball-caps big. Still, you can see how small these buds are and how they settle in deep enough to not be pressed down much when I lay on a pillow.

I was almost planning on returning them before I got them but once I tried them, they are great.

Warning ... easy to lose. They got jostled out of my ear last night and, thankfully, I found them in the bed. My advice to 1More... when you make version 2.0 of these, use fluorescent orange. We are just sleeping with them and that bright color would make them easier to find!

One last thing... Battery life is short which is no surprise given the size of these earbuds. I think they go about 3-4 hours. If you use them to fall asleep and that's it, like me, battery life won't be an issue.

UPDATE 1/1/2022 - Still really like these earbuds for sleep. My biggest complaint is they sometimes fall out overnight so you have to go hunting for them in your bed. Fortunately, I have easily found them every time. Wish they were red or bright pink to make them easier to spot. Not a big deal. Still recommend these!

UPDATE #2: Connectivity issues arose causing one bud to disconnect. Taking off one star. Great customer service though.
title: Stomach-sleepers, side sleepers rejoice - these actually work when your head is on the pillow

review_text:
Sorry about the 3 stars, but I'm not enough of an artist to know whether this product is good or bad, drawing-wise. This review is for prospective Linux users. I have the Intuous CTH-480 model, which has pressure sensitivity and the eraser.

It works for me on openSUSE 13.1 and 12.3, and I expect that it will work on most other Linux if you have access to the necessary packages. You get the software via your Linux distro. The included installation CD is for Windows or Mac, thus useless. The user manual is an online PDF.

You probably don't need (or cannot use, even with WINE) the free downloadable Windows drawing software. But you might as well get it from the Wacom site. On Linux, you would probably use Gimp or Krita for drawing.

Unless your Linux is very new, you probably don't have drivers new enough for this product. No problem, go and get it. It worked for me using kernel 3.14, libwacom 0.9, and xf86-input-wacom-0.22.1 (but not 0.23). I don't know for sure, but am told that kernel-3.11, libwacom-0.7, and xf86-input-wacom-0.20 will suffice. You don't need to upgrade your whole distro, only what you need. If you upgade the kernel, also upgrade the related devel files. Ubuntu users: You might need to install build-essential and files related to Broadcom WiFi, depending on your hardware. See the Ubuntu help site for info.

With the proper packages, my tablet "just worked" the first time. Very nice.

There is a control panel application that lets you customize how the tablet behaves. You don't need it, but it might be useful. You may have to get it from a source outside of your distro. Unfortunately, the necessary packages may not be new enough to recognize this particular model tablet. If you know how, you can compile it from git code using cmake. Be sure to read the README file that comes with the code, since you will have to do some investigation using Terminal and edit a file or two. Worked for me (eventually), but not without pain.

EDIT: In the year since I bought this tablet, the necessary Linux support seems to be more standard, without the need to do your own upgrades. Tablet still works well, even with rough handling.
title: Works with Linux. Read this for some info

I have read far to many reviews about the great sound quality to conclude that there are obviously quite a few people that have lower expectations of sound quality than myself.

The sound from the SoundLink is extremely muddy. The only way I could get acceptable sound was by fiddling with EQ settings from computer or choosing the bass reducer EQ setting on my iPhone. Even then the overall quality is just so so. I will not argue that its sound is not better than the other wireless solutions but then that is not saying much to begin with. I have other Bose products and I expected better sound quality than what this delivers. I am not referring to full volume performance. I am talking about overall sound quality at any level.

It is attractive and portable.. that is about all I can say for it. It will do in a pinch but if I am the only one listening to the music I would not hesitate to use headphones over this.

I give it two stars because of the sound quality vs price. If it had more features like the ability to output to an external amp or a built in EQ to clean up the muddy sound then more of that cost would be justified. This does one thing and for this price it should do it exceptionally.

review_text: I recently had a service related power surge in my power service that burnt out 11 surge suppressors. I bought 13 replacements, this was the only one with a cord I bought. In lightning prone Florida we know that the total number of surge protectors in your home work as one to protect the whole house. I have seen some concerning reviews with photos of soldering defects but now this strip is sold with triangle hole security screws that very few people have drivers for. You can't inspect it before use without the special driver. I have it and mine was OK. The basic design as shown in the description is good, the issue is quality control for the workmanship. The 3 suppressor discs are close together so they will make it very hot in a surge. If the claim of using a high temperature plastic case is true, it should be OK with a large surge. I also see many customer photos of their strips filled with adapters for the 5 volt USB voltage - that is a waste. Unplug your little USB power adapters from the cord and use the 3 provided USB outlets!

review_text:
It's fine. But lacks a few simple features in the app that make it harder to use than it should be.
I only have it on at night. Setting up the schedule is a total PITA with the app. Not intuitive and hard to find where to do it.
During the day, I might bring up a camera if I hear a truck pull up to see if it is the UPS. This takes forever. Usually the guy is pulling away or GONE before the camera comes on. Just too slow.
If I hear shouting, I also want to take a look out front. Sometimes, I want to record it. But there is NO WAY to quickly record something you are viewing. Indeed, I have no idea HOW. In viewing only mode, they need a big, red record arrow so you can record the event. Also, in the app, that instant record needs to be a different default time than the other viewing time. The camera shuts off very fast but if two dopes are fighting, I need that camera to record for 5 minutes minimum.
The detection is OK but not as good as it could be. I do detect raccoons and cats on my back deck and it records them but, again, it is so slow, it is just a moment of the animal.
Since I do not have them on all the time, the batteries do last a long, long time in a 4 season climate. My first of these I use the most, just pooped out after a few years. I dropped in some OLD Li AA batteries I had laying around and, they have held up great. So you do get a long time out of the batteries doing night only activation and occasional use during day.
Only two of my cameras come with some free cloud storage. One does not. I bought these because I do not want to pay for that. There really needs to be a way to store it to your macOS or iOS device.
In conclusion, I think now there are better options. Do more research before jumping at this Amazon product.

review_text: The caption on the box says it all – “The Best Gife For You”.  If a spelling error like that makes it into production you know the product is likely to be cheaply made, and I found that that’s the case here.  I’m comparing these with some speakers that I picked up from Monoprice.  I first played music through these speakers and felt as if I was listening to a very “plastic-y” music – it almost sounded like the bass-less sound you’d expect from a grocery store speaker.  The sound is there and it sounds OK, but it definitely doesn’t sound “good”.  I have Bluetooth, battery powered speakers that cost around $20 that have a higher quality sound than these speakers do.  Compared to the Monoprice speakers these sound very high-pitched.  The Monoprice speakers sound much richer.  I figured that maybe by adding a subwoofer the quality of sound from these speakers wouldn’t be noticeably different when compared to the Monoprice speakers, so I purchased a subwoofer to test with these.  Unfortunately, while I now have lots of bass, the sound doesn’t “mesh” – I have a distinct base and a distinct upper-frequency sound coming from these speakers.  With the Monoprice speakers the sound blends much better.  I also compared these to the Herdio 6.5” ceiling speakers and 5.25” ceiling speaker.  These sound better than both of those speakers.  Overall, these aren’t bad at $30 each, but I can’t recommend them compared to other brands, unfortunately.

review_text:
Lets be clear, I love my surface pro 3. Its a great little laptop/tablet. I'm a photographer and have loaded photoshop and lightroom and lots of plug-ins and the thing is fast and beautiful. But it cries out for a keyboard and the fact that it doesn't come with one is just plain silly. Actually more than silly.... its downright maddening. I wouldn't have minded if microsoft has bundled the surface with a cheap keyboard that could be upgradeable to something fancier, but to call this thing a laptop or desktop replacement and then sell it without a keyboard is just wrong.

So, I bought this Cyan type cover. Obviously being made by microsoft, it fits the surface pro 3 quite well. It types well and has big enough keys that I don't feel like I am typing on a lillipution keyboard. The track pad is decent enough as track pads go. I hear it is a huge improvement of the last cover microsoft put out The blue color is lovely. When closed around the surface it shuts down the display which is excellent and it gives good protection for the glass. So, in all these ways it is a great cover/keyboard. You

So what's my complaint? Why is this a fabric? Its like a weird fake suede or some other fabric that is an absolute dust magnet. I live with a few four legged creatures and it is next to impossible for this keyboard to live here without attracting loose fur, and dust. I am also not hopeful that it will last very long without looking terribly ratty. After 2 weeks it is already starting to show signs of wear. And because it is this weird fabric you have to be very very very careful where you put this down. Make sure whatever surface you are placing it on is absolutely clean because if not, whatever dust or dirt it rests on will be transfered to this cover. You can't just wipe it off the way you could with a smooth plastic or metal cover. Honestly, if I was working for microsoft I would have demoted -- if not fired -- the engineers who designed this. Or perhaps they are being given raises because the faster this keyboard gets ruined the more replacement sales there will be.

There is one other minor complaint.... the pen holder loop that you are supposed to somehow stick onto the cover fell off before the first day was over. I have no idea if I simply got a defective one or whether others have had the same problem but it is a stupid little thing that this isn't somehow better built into the cover.

As I said, to call this an optional accessory is absolutely ludicrous. You just can't use this as the serious computer microsoft touts it as being without a keyboard. Grrrrrrrr.

BOTTOM LINE: Works well, good trackpad, Horrible fabric, but it's the cover that fits the surface so you might as well spring for it if you want to do serious computing.
title: Good Cover and keyboard.  Horrible material.

review_text:
PROS:
*Lightweight (lighter than most flashlights)
*Good battery life
*Stable when upright (good shape and weight balance)
*Seems to be fairly durable
*Handle on top works for hanging or carrying with one or two fingers (or you can easily attach a lanyard to it if you want a wrist strap), and the handle folds down and nestles smoothly into the top of the lantern when not in use
*Back plate pops into place when raised (there is a button to release it), so it does not fall down when you want it up
*Yellow color makes it easier to find in your bag than black/darker colored flashlights

CONS:
*Not bright enough for most uses, and the light has a very small range. Not terrible when lighting a small tent enough to find things, get dressed, etc. but we don't recommend this when walking or when you need focused light
*The back plate that is designed to direct the light forward doesn't make as much of a difference as we expected
*You need two hands to move the back plate back down (one to push the button and one to push the plate down)
*Feels awkward when carrying by the body like you would with a flashlight (carrying by the handle is much less awkward)
title: Some good features, but simply not bright enough

Used iPads as old as the one we have are not very expensive, but I wanted to keep the one we had since new going for a few more years. I ordered this kit and then watched the video. Seeing Apple had used an adhesive to secure things into place and really provided no easy way to get to the battery was a major red flag. I had already ordered the kit, so I had to try.

The kit itself is just simple cheap tools, shims, a couple of wipes and new adhesive in addition to the battery. All the tools combined probably cost a quarter or fifty cents at the most to make. I was fine with going online to get instructions and watching the video. The video is edited, so you really do not see how much of a pain in the rear it is to get the screen glass off. It took me about fifteen minutes to get three shims in place and on the forth, the glass shattered. What an epic waste of time and money and rather than having a dying iPad, we now had a dead one.

Unless you just have to have your iPad live a few more years and cannot buy a used one a years newer or better yet, a brand new one, do not bother with doing this. We have a 2020 iPad Pro, so now I have to wonder if that will ever be able to get the battery replaced, but we got nine years at this iPad that is now dead.

review_text:
I liked the features of this product. It will act as a NAS, and it comes with software that will allow you to automatically backup your important files to the drive (purchased separately) installed. It is large, but relatively attractive in style. Setup was simple and straight forward. WiFi coverage is more than adequate for my home which is not large. It supports AirPrint and a number of other convenient features. It comes with an application to help you manage it which is easy to use and relatively useful. The app is a bit of "bloatwear" though, and seems to embed itself into the wireless management of Windows which is unnecessary and unwelcome, though almost everyone who gets the chance to do so seems to do this.
Unfortunately, this is when the positive stops.
After 4 months of operation, the Ethernet port that connects it to the cable modem and ultimately the Internet has failed. I contacted their support staff via a web chat session. While typing in the description of the problem to their tech, he felt the need to let me know that if I didn't finish in 3 minutes time he would disconnect me.
This message left me with the warm feeling that the management of their silly call center is more interested in managing their numbers than servicing their customers. Nice.
Shortly into my chat session with support from NetGear, the tech sent me the following message...

"Neil: Please be informed that your WNDR4700 has 90 days of Support Warranty and 1 year of Hardware Warranty from the date of purchase, which was on Feb 27, 2015.
Please be informed that the device is already beyond the 90 days of Support Warranty from its date of purchase..."

I guess the intent here on the part of NetGear is to hedge their bet on the hardware warranty. It appears to me that the purpose is to have you pay them for "Support" in order to identify a hardware failure rendering the hardware warranty useless.
Never the less (This is the only positive part of the experience.), the tech I was web chatting with didn't ask for money and we proceeded. I suspect that when I call their support number, I'll find that I'll need to pay them somehow once they figure out I've had the AP more than 90 days.
Ultimately the tech came to the conclusion that suddenly after 4 months of the AP operating normally, my ISP (Xfinity) has suddenly decided to only accept traffic from the MAC address of my computer, and what I really need to do is configure MAC Spoofing to solve the problem.
In order to come to the conclusion above, I think it's a fair assumption that NetGear and/or their tech believes Xfinity isn't smart enough to use the MAC address of the cable modem to identify my home, they really need to identify a MAC address on the other side of the cable modem to ensure they have a contract with their customer and/or Xfinity still believes most of their customers still have a desktop or tower directly connected to their network without the use of a firewall of some sort and/or WiFi.
The configuration of MAC spoofing seems to require a hard Ethernet connection to the AP so that the AP can copy my MAC address. This connection causes the connection to the Internet through my iPhone's hot spot to fail.
Of course, conveniently, he only does web chat support and there’s no way for him to call me or have someone else call me and he has to disconnect from me leaving me to follow the silly MAC spoofing instructions and I guess I'm supposed to call their support number, wait on hold for who knows how long, only to start the same silly game over.
Obviously the silly MAC spoofing plan didn't work.
The only question remaining is: "Should I pursue them to replace the failing device while spending a few more hours on the phone "troubleshooting", only to possibly have another device fail, or do I cut my losses and move on to a device from another company?".
title: The Support and Warranty on this Device is Horrible

These are the first set of Bluetooth headphones I have purchased and I use it only for working out and therefore my assessment is based on that. I have had these headphones for one month and work out everyday.

-Has a tendency to feel like it is slipping out of your ears while running or doing highly intensive workouts if you sweat profusely.

review_text:
Bought this router based on the wonderful reviews after my 5+ year old Linksys router started dropping the connection.
Purchased October 16, 2011 (found the receipt over the weekend), died January 23, 2012. Set up is about as far from "intuitive, plug and play" as it can be. Had problems early on with my laptop, keeping the laptop wireless (everything else in the house worked wirelessly.) Called Customer Service, reached a call center in another country. Technician was unfriendly,condescending and impossible to understand. After 30 minutes, essentially hung up on me after telling me the problem was my laptop and to call Dell. ~CLICK~.
Just got a new computer 2 weeks ago. Had tech savvy nephew hook everything up for me. Worked fine for about 5 days (even the printer was wireless again, hooray!) and then one morning it worked, that same night, the router just died. NOTHING worked anymore, even though the wireless adapter tirelessly tried to establish a connection. Called customer service again this weekend. Different representative, worse service. The language barrier clearly went both ways, as I had to spell everything (name, address, email,etc.) I finally lost it when he said very snidely: "I'm sure it's there ma'am. Internet. I N T E R N E T." I hung up before I said something I'd be embarrassed about later on when I cooled off. Tech savvy nephew came back. Tried multiple times, uninstalled, reinstalled updated drivers, software, etc. Nothing. Router is effectively dead barely 90 days after I purchased it.
I was told this sort of hardware isn't designed to last more than a year-18 months tops. I think 3 months is unacceptable.
Guess what I ordered for a router tonight? Yep, you guessed it, a Linksys.
Belkin--never EVER again.
title: Horrible product, even worse customer service

review_text:
I've tried many Blutooth headsets (Mono only until this one.)
Most recently the highly rated Jawbone ERA. It was just OK at first, but had trouble hearing the other party. After about a month the mic broke and it didn't work at all. So what to get after that?

I liked the fact that I could use this to listen to music as well as make calls, so I thought I'd give it a try.

PROS:
No more complaining from the other party about audio quality, which i've had at times with every other headset I've used.
In noisy environments I can use both earbuds while on calls which effectively blocks out ambient noise.
They seem very rugged and well-built.
There's plenty of volume, I have no trouble hearing the other party even with just one earbud in.
They are great for listening to music in the gym.

CONS:
I seem to be getting about 3 hours of talk time vs. the 5 hours advertised. There's a charging case available, I did not purchase it.
A little awkward to use in situations where you only want one earbud in.
Expected, but the audio quality for music isn't as good as wired high fidelity earbuds. (That's not really the purpose of these though.)

Overall, I'd highly recommend these to anyone who wants a stereo Bluetooth headset.
title: All time best Bluetooth headset I've owned.

This is my first after market radio since high school when you were defined by you're car. I needed one because my new to me work truck (2000 ram 3500 CTD) had a really bad head unit with no AUX.

First off, the main con. Its cheap, like everything these days it just feels like you're gonna break it in you're hand. The face is extremely light and cheap feeling.

Pros - Well, it works really well.
-The interface is a bit clumsy (as are all of these smaller units without larger screens) but once you get it configured its done
-The color changing is cool, I was able to find a green that matched my trucks dash and gauge light closes enough for my approval.
-BT works extremely well with my iPhone, audio sound great (better that I expected for BT) It give you a lot of good options like auto connect on/off, auto play on/off, and good control over you're player.
-USB works on my iPhone, I'm not sure it explained that on the box of descriptions. I thought it would only work on Android when I bought it (other than charging) but it is able to play audio over USB form my iPhone and control it. Apps like Pandora have a "accessory mode" and this device take over full control. very cool
-Charging, not sure what its USB charging specs are but it seems to charge my iPhone 6 very well.
-No CD - I didn't want one, much cleaner...
-Sound - better than my stock head unit, but I did change out my door speakers at the same time

Anyways, Its not terribly high end, but it works well enough. Im happy with it.
title: I needed one because my new to me work truck (2000 ram 3500 CTD) had a really bad head unit with no AUX

When she visited last, while she played some game on the tablet, I remembered why I bought it in the first place.  It has a 2560x1600 monitor on it.  That screen is crystal clear.  I can't imagine why anyone would even consider buying a 1900x1200 monitor.  The higher density is so much more vivid, and no pixilization.  This pops between aps nicely, and remembers where you were in an ap you had visited, that's nice because I read something, then want to explore further on the net, so you can bounce back and forth nicely.  The ap I use the most is the AutoDesk Sketch program.  I paid the extra $3.99 for the upgrade to pro and have been happy, happy, happy.  It's like a miniature PhotoSuite.  It is fast, quite, turns on when I open the cover, turns off when I close it, remembers where it was, and has a ton of useful aps.  This tablet goes with me everywhere. I own 2  PC tablets, and 8 PC Desktops I like this the best. Thanks Jeff, this is a hit.  When are you going to make this in a 12" screen?

review_text: Lots of good reviews here, Consumers Reports, too.  However, either no one thinks this is important, or there are some really poorly focusing examples of this camera out in the wild. An image almost is brought into focus, then it goes out, and stays there.  My first and last adventure with this camera was a wedding.  I took many available light photos, that were clearly viewable in the viewfinder.  Roughly half of them were out of focus, or the focus was on a part of the image that wasn't in "the box".  This camera replaced a 7 year old Olympus Camedia that died.  The Camedia never had this problem with focus.  Reviews discussing shutter lag indicate it is due to focusing taking place after the shutter is pressed.  In that event, with the lag being described as under two-tenths of a second, it would seem that focusing should be very quick, very accurate.  Not in the example camera I had.  One other Amazon review mentions focus issues similar to mine.  No one else.  I've returned mine (to Target), and I'm afraid to get another.  I'll keep looking.

review_text:
Update Nov 16, 2020: Samsung finally reached out to me and a member of their engineering team who works on these projectors called. Clearly knowledgeable. We are working on the focus issue and how to resolve, if possible. Seen some improvement but still not "perfect". That said the LSP7T is far better than the Optoma P1 or P2 and I would not hesitate to recommend it to anyone vs any of the other sub-4k USTs on the market.

Update Nov 6, 2020: Now going on 4 hours spent trying to find a Samsung technical representative that handles these projectors. Spoke to over 10 reps, transferred every time and none say they know anything about these UST projectors. Constant run around and there is NO WAY to reach anyone other than overseas who reads from a script.

Original review: I received the projector on October 24th. So far the experience has been pretty good but there are a few issues that I have with the projector that Samsung needs to address before I can rate this thing "5 stars" for the money.

First the good:
1. Vivid picture with good colors for a projector. I can compare this to the Optoma P1 and P2 and say that it has better picture quality imo, not by a huge amount but enough to give it an edge.
2. Software platform is rock solid as you would expect from Samsung. Again, comparing to Optoma it's a night and day difference.
3. Connection/HDMI stability is also super rock solid with no issues whatsoever on a variety of sources. In my configuration I'm using a Denon AVC8500H connected to a CAAVO Control Center (and also with the Caavo removed) with multiple sources tested at 4k 60hz and lower resolutions: Xbox One X, Nvidia Shield Pro, Fire TV Stick 4k and Cube, Nintendo Switch and W10 PC with Geforce 2080ti at 4k 60hz. All ran without a hitch. Great!
4. Used with an Elite Screens CLR (not the 2 or 3, just the CLR). Great combo. Daytime (slightly light controlled room) and night both looked great (with nighttime obviously looking fantastic).
5. Fan noise is non-existent. Completely silent.
6. Projector turns on and shuts down perfectly with CEC control.
7. Start up time is in seconds (haven't directly timed it but I would put it around 10 seconds). Very good imo.

Cons:
1. Focus issues at the corners and edges from mid to top. It's enough to be distracting on content with text, lines or other details where sharpness is important. I'm working on contacting Samsung about the issue.
2. Some shadow crushing in live content especially in scenes that are generally darkly lit. Not "bad" but as with the focus enough to be distracting. Could be due to calibration but I think it's the nature of the projector. It is not enough for me to dislike the projector it's just something I wish was better.

Overall I like the projector more and more as I use it, especially when comparing to the Optoma units I had previously (the P1 and P2). However the focus issue needs addressed and imo should not be present in a $3300 projector. I will update once I hear back from Samsung.

Lastly I may move up to the LSP9T at some point depending on what I hear back from Samsung on the focus issue and how much better the blacks/shadows might be on the more expensive unit.
title: Good and bad.  Generally a good first attempt with a couple of issues to fix

review_text:
This flash drive feels like an early-release product that could benefit from some refinement. It’s great that both type-A and -C ports are offered, in the same-sized housing as a regular USB drive, but the design isn’t as convenient as it could be. Likewise, the drive offers superb read performance, but its writing speed leaves much to be desired. Physically, the device consists of a stubby USB-A flash drive, a metal USB A-to-C adapter, and a plastic USB-C cap. It’s a nice design, but there’s room for improvement.

Both the USB-A drive and end cap offer little texture and can be hard to grip (e.g., if your hands have lotion on them). The USB-C plug doesn’t extend far out the adapter’s wide housing, so it may not fit into recessed/tight areas (such as the USB port of a phone inside a case). The cap snaps onto the back of the device, keeping everything together while using the USB-C port, but that’s not the case while using the other port. The adapter has nowhere to go while using USB-A, so it ends up being one more thing to keep track of.

In use, this 64GB drive’s performance is unbalanced, and whether or not that’s a problem depends on how you intend to use it. Reading zips along at 200-225 MB/s, but the write speed is slow and uneven. While copying files to the drive, it rapidly bounces between 10 and 30 MB/s, averaging just around 20 MB/s. That’s a rather disappointing result for a modern USB 3.x flash drive.

Overall, there are some good (if somewhat unpolished) ideas in this flash drive’s design, but it’s tough to recommend given the slow write speeds. The larger capacity versions (128/256GB) might offer better performance, but I can’t say for sure without testing them.
title: Clever but imperfect design, fast read speed but slow at writing

review_text:
This device captures video directly to SD card from component (NOT COMPOSITE!) or HDMI. I got great help from tech support to set up the capture software on my PC as well. The LED’s on the box are important (no info is included with the unit to explain the LED) so here’s what you need to know:
PWR:
Flashes blue when first powering up or switching modes (booting).
This LED will continue to flash blue if the driver is not present, or has an issue on the PC as well.

Solid Blue when ready.

Input:
Blue: HDMI
Amber: Component

Mode:
Blue: PC
Amber: SD Card
White (Pink): Network (Standalone)

SD Card:
Blue: Ready to capture.
Purple: Not a valid file system.
Flashing Purple: Reading/Writing to SD Card.

The Dual LED’s on either side of the record button:
Flashing red: Error condition (No network, no source, can’t start capture)
Flashing Blue: The unit is recording or streaming.
Solid Purple: HDMI input signal is HDCP protected. Unit will not record or stream.
title: What the LED’s mean (important)

review_text:
Excellent price but just "so-so" design. The item arrived by regular USPS delivery about 5 days later than the original projected delivery date. That was annoying to begin with because my new iPad was delivered much earlier than expected and I was afraid to use it without the added protection of a case. The packaging was a simple vinyl envelope with no padding inside. The screen protector had been punched away from the case itself but still had a glued surface so I was able to reattach it. The case had no instructions included and I was not able to locate anything on the iBlason site to show assembly but if you have had a similar style case in the past it is not difficult to figure out. It snapped together fairly easily and is a perfect fit for the iPad air. The silicone sleeve slipped on easily too. After using it for a few days, I don't notice much "bulk" to it. The iPad still feels light and slim in my hands. The stand is very difficult to open with just my finger tips. I assume I should be using a coin or something to pry it loose from the back of the case. In portrait mode it is almost useless. Every time I swipe from left to right the device falls over. It is not well balanced. In landscape mode it is much better.
For only $15 this is an acceptable case. I wish it had been an Amazon Prime available purchase. I know it would have come on time and in much better packaging direct fom Amazon. Rumor is the Otterbox may be available in January and I will probably upgrade then. For the price though this was a good buy!

It is now the end of Feb. this product has held up better than expected. I have gotten use to the problem of it tipping over in portrait mode. It is still annoying, but I'll live with it for the price. The stand opens easier now. I guess it just needed to get broken in. It has protected my iPad from grandchildren ages 2, 3, and 10 with no problems. I adjusted my rating from 3 to 4 stars and I'm happier with my purchase now. I've decided to stick with this rather than give up the $100 for an Otterbox.
title: Great price

review_text:
Been using this for a few days and so far so good. My daily commute is in the suburbs so I can leave it in Highway mode and not get too many false alarms.

However, even though it works well from an alert standpoint, there is a huge flaw with the design. Not being able to dim the indicators is one thing but not being able to turn off the two bright blue lights on top of the device is a real problem.

This time of the year, my commute is dark in both directions. When the detector goes off, those blue lights are extremely visible to any vehicle near me. That means if I wasn't speeding, which I'm not most of the time, an officer can still see that I obviously have a radar detector. Although it's not illegal in PA (as of this review, radar detectors are only contraband in VA and DC), I feel totally uncomfortable alerting officers that I have this. Potentially, even when I'm driving speed limit, they could find a reason to pull me over and write me a citation for windshield obstruction. Oh, how ironic and tragic it would be!

I'm still keeping this device since it works well but I'll be adding some electrical tape to cover up those blue lights. The blue lights are meant to grab your attention, not others within a quarter mile radius. If a blue light was on a short wire dangling below the dash, that would be perfect. Minus 1 star due to not being able to turn those off.
title: Great detector but you need to cover the blue lights

Pros: -The items came well packaged....double boxed/padded.

Cons: -Picture quality is very sub-par for a 4K monitor. Not even remotely comparable to other 4K monitors I own/use.

-The unit I received came with several dead pixels in the upper left of the screen..... visible when I conducted a
dead pixel test using the color gambit.

For some time I have been considering the monitors from MonoPrice, trying to decide if they were a solid buy, or just more imported junk. This monitor falls in the middle, leaning more towards the junk side..... For the cost, It's simply impossible to qualify it as a solid value, and the poor implementation and location of the controls adds to the con list. In addition, the last straw for me is that this monitor supposedly carries a "perfect pixel" guarantee... meaning NO DEAD PIXELS..... then when you try to get support/replacement under that policy, the policy changes, and/or your support request it ignored. Stick with a well known brand, and don't waste your money on this monitor.

review_text:
You can use this antenna without or with the amplifier. The manufacturer recommends starting without. This antenna gave really sharp pictures on some channels -- but nothing on other channels. I tried different positions and orientations to find the best set of channels. Then we tried adding the amplifier -- and we got no picture at all. (The manufacturer says the amplifier may cause something like "echo oscillation" if the signal is strong. We were using this in a major city, Denver. Whatever: the amplifier didn't help. The $17 Philips non-amplified antenna we'd been using did pretty well, which tells me that there's plenty of signal in the area... maybe enough to cause that "echo oscillation".)

We ended up using the "HD Digital TV Antenna up to 120+ Miles Range by UJM, Indoor HDTV Antenna with Amplifier Signal Booster Support ...", which did a fabulous job: good enough without the amplifier, but even better with it. I suggest trying a few antennas. Maybe this one would work better with the amplifier in more-rural areas that *don't* have a strong signal?
title: Better than nothing without the amplifier, worse with the amplifier
