review_text:
Purchased at Fry's Electronics, as Amazon was back ordered at the time (Fry's is my #2 retailer behind Amazon.com because of their great return policy).

I had the Bose SoundLink II Wireless Over‑Ear, but ended up returning them because the sound was a bit lacking.

Enter the Bose QuietComfort 35 Wireless.

All I have to say is WOW. Absolutely top-notch noise cancellation and, wait for it...SOUND! I have several other BT headphones and these are at the top of the food chain sound-wise, even without taking into consideration the peerless noise cancellation, which take these to a level of their own. I am NOT an audio purist, I just like clean sound with "life" and a nice bass/sub-bass response.

To compare, I have the following BT headphones right now: B&O H7 (aptX), V-Moda Crossfade Wireless, and Plantronics Backbeat Pro (aptX). I have been heavy into BT headphones the last 6 months, so my opinions have evolved the more BT headphones I've listened to, which is almost everything on the market, with the exception of the Master & Dynamic MW60s.

Sound is subjective, but I've tried to be as objective as possible with the following attributes: Clarity, Soundstage, Imaging, Bass

EQUIPMENT USED
iPhone 6s - Apple Music & Google Play
LG G4 (aptX) - Apple Music & Google Play

CLARITY
1) Bose QuietComfort 35
2) B&O H7
3) Plantronics Backbeat Pro
4) V-Moda Crossfade Wireless

The Bose win here. The sound is clean with virtually no artifacts, while the H7s are a close 2nd. The Plantronics are clean, but it seems to miss some frequencies. The V-Modas have strong mids, but slightly muddy upper frequency range in comparison with the others.

SOUNDSTAGE
1) Bose QuietComfort 35
2) B&O H7
3) Plantronics Backbeat Pro
4) V-Moda Crossfade Wireless

Again, Bose takes the cake, which was a little surprising. Whatever DSP Bose is using, it's definitely been refined from the SoundLink II Wireless Over‑Ears and presents an unexpectedly wide soundstage, not just for a closed back headphone, but even compared to my open back Sennheiser HD 518s.

IMAGING
1) Bose QuietComfort 35
2) B&O H7
3) V-Moda Crossfade Wireless
4) Plantronics Backbeat Pro

I fully expected the B&O H7s to win here, but I was again very impressed with the QC 35s at how each instrument sounded full, yet separate from each other instrument. This is quite an impressive feat, considering the QC 35s do not have aptX.

BASS
1) Bose QuietComfort 35
2) B&O H7
3) V-Moda Crossfade Wireless
4) Plantronics Backbeat Pro

This one was a bit tricky, since it's more subjective than the other categories. For me, I enjoy a tight bass with nice sub-bass rumble when called for, but not an over-powering bass. For me, the QC 35s have the best quality & quantity of bass, while the H7s are a close 2nd and mirror the QC 35s, but just not quite as good. The V-Modas definitely have the highest quantity of bass (punchy), but it's lacks the same quality of sub-bass rumble and can get just slightly sloppy. The BBPs have very good bass response, both in quality & quantity, but the reason I ranked them last on this list is because when the bass hits, it seems to drown out other frequency ranges.

CONCLUSION
The Bose QuietComfort 35, to me, is the best BT headphone on the market right now, both in terms of noise cancellation and impressive sound. As you can see in the photo, I also have a wired Sony MDR-1A, which I compared to the QC 35s. While the MDR-1As sounded better, which is expected because they are a high-end wired headphone, I found the QC 35s came shockingly close to the MDR-1As.

TWO THUMBS UP!
title: 5 Star Noise Cancellation AND Sound

review_text:
One of the better projectors I've used in a long time! I also purchased the "refurbished" model, so my review is based upon that.

(+): Compact, lightweight, full HD resolution, works well in both bright and dim environments. For the price, this projector can't be beat. I use this for travel and it's been absolutely exceptional. Image quality is far better than some of the more expensive Sony and Optoma projectors on the market. While the lumen count may be a bit lower than others, it definitely doesn't show and actually appears to be brighter. If you use this projector on the go, you'll appreciate the minimal to no "cool down" time that most projectors have.

(-): Auto-leveling feature can act a little strange when you use the front leg to prop up (takes some fiddling with), menu controls seem a bit slow/laggy when using the remote or hardware buttons. Included carrying case is very thin and offers little to no protection. Minor aesthetic gripe; why include a flat/off-white remote with a piano black device? It doesn't even look like they match.

Overall, it's a great bargain, both at the new and refurbished price points. Replacement bulbs can be found at around $100, which is cheaper than most rivals. Highly recommended!
title: Excellent Projector!

I have been hearing so many good things about this tablet, and android KitKat, that I finally purchased one.
The resolution of the screen is beautiful, snapdragon processor is snappy,and Kit Kat brings some nice albeit minor changes to android.
That's where my love affair with Nexus 7 ends. Two major issues plagued the 32GB version of the tablet:
First the keyboard and multi-touch have a problem. When using the built in Google virtual keyboard, most of the time I would get the wrong character or additional characters from what I typed. This was most problematic when trying to log in to a site with my password as I kept getting an error that my account and password did not match.. That's because the keyboard was adding additional letters to the ones I typed. For example, instead of "Password" it would add characters or type wrong ones so I would get something like "] PPasddewoerdd"
I also had issues with wifi connectivity for Internet based apps and streaming content where I would get an error message "APP has stopped suddenly" or I would just get thrown out of a video.
Another pet peeve of mine is the large bezel at the bottom of the screen which made a 7" screen look smaller than tablets with more of an edge to edge design.
I have returned it and am sticking with my Samsung Galaxy Tab 8 inch, which has proven very reliable. The slim design and additional useable screen real estate of the Tab3 8.0 outshines the overall performance of the new Asus designed Nexus 7.
Maybe I got a defective one, but from some Web searches the problems seem somewhat widespread, and apparently Google is aware of the issues but have yet to issue an update to fix them. Disappointed that performance didn't measure up to all the accolades of the tech media who seem to be in love with Google and Apple and extra critical of perhaps the industry's most innovative performer, Samsung.
title: Hype is nice, but Performance is what counts

review_text:
The sound quality is reasonable for headphones of this price range. I mainly listen to classical music. I wouldn't say the sound is great, but it's not bad either - just average.

Noise cancelling works fairly well too. I wore these headphones during a flight and I'd say the headphones cut down the plane noise level by at least 50%. The ANC does take a bit of getting used to though because the "quietness" feels somewhat unnatural, but after a while I almost don't notice it.

The ear pads are soft and comfortable. It's important to adjust the pads so that they envelop the ear lobes completely. If the pads sit on top of some parts of my ear lobes, I find my ears start to hurt after a while. The pads aren't very breathable. After wearing them for about 2 hours my ears would get very hot and sweaty that I have to take them off.

My biggest complaint is that these headphones make a strong echo during phone calls. This is due to the fact (a faulty design?) that the microphone is right next to the left-ear speaker so that every sound coming out of the left-ear speaker gets picked up by the microphone and sent back down the line. The result is that the other person on the line would hear their own words sent back to them with a few seconds of delay, which makes it impossible to carry on a conversation.
title: echo during phone calls

review_text:
By "noise cancelling" I mean that the boom mike clearly picks up your voice, but unlike a regular "stick" microphone it does not pick up all the background room noise - You might get a little if the noise is particularly loud, but things like air-conditioning or hard drives or CPU fan noise doesn't come through. (The fan noise from an HP server starting up might come through but that sounds like a jet taking off). My point is that I used to use a stick mike and one of the things I found annoying was that you could hear when the air from the heating vent started or stopped, and you could hear the hard drive.

Comfort-wise, the length of the band can be adjusted if your ears are farther apart, and the foam cushions make it possible to wear these a few hours without pinching my ears. (Your experience may differ, but I've had ear phones that were either too tight or pads that were too small or inadequate cushion - these were comfortable to wear for 5-6 hours).

The boom mike will swivel from +120 degrees to -120 degrees, so you can wear the mike on your left or right side by swiveling it around.

Volume-wise these headsets seemed a bit quieter than my speakers, so I had to crank the volume up on the PC. The cord has a built-in volume adjustment, but I left this cranked up all the way.

On the other end of this particular model it has two 3.5mm plugs - one green, and one pink. I chose this particular model because it had those separate connectors -the green "headset" connector goes into my computer's output, and I use the pink connector on a Sony PVR so that I can record my voice separately. But you could easily plug both cables into the front audio jacks found on most PCs.

I left off one star because the range of audio isn't as good as a professional mike and the construction doesn't seem that strong, but for the price this is an excellent product - I am currently using this as an entry level mike in the field of computer videos.
title: Great noise-cancelling headset

review_text:
I recently become fervent about Bluetooth devices after trying to watch movies at night with my wife and ways of not to disturbing our 1 year-old. This day and age we are stucked with radiofrequency and Bluetooth option. RF devices are around for a while and gives good range for home entertainment. Interference is a potential from home phones. Bluetooth on the other hand is more versatile in terms of portability and multiple devices application. Investment for Bluetooth home system at this level is about 150 for my Priva II + 2 Audition headset. If go RF then Senheiser's RS 120 runs about the same at 140 for a pair. So I decide on Bluetooth because of the portability of the headphones with my iPhone. Hence, I narrow down a few things for decision:
-price
-range
-latency
-sound quality

I obtained both MEE and Priva II for comparison (paid full price, no discount or free sampling). They are very similar products, and compare as below:
-both are compact, can be battery operate for hours, similar price range, similar transmission range (I'll describe later) and connect up to 2 Bluetooth devices

What's up with Priva II?
Pro:
-smaller, slight cheaper
-it remembers your connected Bluetooth devices, so no need to re-pairing each time
-magnet base can somehow stick onto nearby electronics for ease of positioning
-better sound quality (tested with movies, musical, and bass test songs from YouTube and on two different Bluetooth headphone) that I can discern
Con:
-some paint chipped off on the multifunction button as arrived
-cheaper looking package
-no Toslink/optical connection

What's up with MEE?
Pro:
-good package, the device is black and looks great with my TV set
-Toslink capability, which my relatively old smart TV has only. I had to connect either through my Yamaha receiver or computer directly, which can be cumbersome.
Con:
-more expensive
-less sound quality (only after when I compare with Priva II in order to tell the difference)
-need to pair every time when turn on (this takes a few seconds, but gets very annoying and inconvenient)

What about range of transmission?
I tested it specifically because my first pairs of tiny MPOW Bluetooth headphone keeps dropping when connected in dual mode. When connected to a single device, there is really no major difference between the two pieces. I was able to get around 20 feet, but doesn't penetrate brick wall. When connected to 2 Bluetooth devices, I got signal drops even just sitting in front of the TV on my couch, which is about 6-7 feet away. Then I switch to another pair of headphone from Avantree (MPOW gives 25 feet in no obstacle, Avantree Audition about 40 feet). This time it's better, single pair I can now get up to 20 feet and about 10-12 feet on dual. This seems to be the issue with both in dual mode and the distance is approximately halved. Priva II probably gives an extra foot or two after multiple testing and walking in my apartment. I guess headphone's baseline Bluetooth range determines how far you can go. Both of my headphone sets are Aptx capable and I couldn't tell any latency in both single and dual mode on both devices.

Bluetooth wireless option is great for home theater with added benefit to turn your phone into wireless as well, which I enjoy a lot during my commute to work. The pitfall is the range cut off as compare with conventional RF device.

MEE or Priva II? They are comparable and just different style in appearance. MEE is more manly and solid looking while Priva is more tech-looking. Sound quality is definitely better on Priva II and the design with magnet base is unique.

I ended up choosing Priva II for the above reasons and one star off for no Toslink and the chipped paint on the multifunction (maybe the packaging too, but hey, it's 10 bucks cheaper). Recommend for anyone who wants to go wireless and doesn't care about Toslink!
title: Priva II or MEE Dual Stream?

I was so excited to receive this computer. I had previously had a chromebook and was looking forward to returning to Windows and an actual file storage system within the computer. $1,000, I assumed this laptop would pack a punch. Unfortunately, this computer seems to be a lemon. my computer usage is pretty basic, it tends toward watching media, email, reading articles, spreadsheets, and holding voice conferences. I assume that on a professional computer video and audio would be powerful. The video was only 720, and automatically placed an extremely strong and strange looking filter over my face. It says you can remove it entirely, but removing it entirely and sending it to zero it was still very clear that a level of filter still existed. The filter looked very obvious and weird. for a laptop and at professionals, this will most certainly make you look unprofessional immediately.

I've also had problems with the audio. I wasn't able to hold Zoom meetings without using a completely separate microphone and speakers as no one could hear me clearly with the laptop alone, and their sound levels were poor as well. after messing with the controls for a very long time I came to the conclusion that the built-in microphone and video camera are just a poor quality.

I didn't use the computer for a few days. It was unplugged but charged up, and I put it back into its box to protected from it from dust until I came back to mess with the computer again and try to find more positive things to say about it. when I opened the computer, the screen was completely frozen on some strange golden static screen with a black bar accross it. it would not respond to ctrl-alt-delete or anything other than holding my thumb on the touch sensor button until it shut down.

The computer did eventually come back when I restarted it, but the computer is already breaking down for no reason about a week into ownership! some of the other reviews I read, it sounds like I didn't get a lemon, but instead this is a problem throughout the entire product line.

Perhaps this is something that can be resolved and maybe the strength of his computer wouldn't be lost on someone who games more or has a more technical skill set than I do. But no matter how much you know about computers I still assume that no one would enjoy having theirs crash before a single download ever took place, or much web surfing, or anything else that could corrupt the computer.

The computer is thin, lightweight, and attractively designed. Those are unfortunately the only good things I have to say about it.

While I have poor vision, I do not use braille or other visual aides beyond glasses. However I thought this would be an interesting way for me to add a more tactile feel to my new ergo keyboard which has keys in weird shapes, sizes, and placements. Given this use case I didn't apply the whole kit and I think people who want a full keyboard of braille will be disappointed. I assume things like "Windows key", left/right arrows, braces and brackets, etc exist in braille however some of these stickers are completely missing here. I was able to repurpose other stickers for things I actually wanted to feel (like F2 and F4 for brackets since they actually make that shape when rotated.)

At the end of the day I think these are better than other solutions I've come across. Dome stickers, nail polish over a piece of sand, hand cut pieces of tape, all lack the distinction and clean look of these stickers. I knocked off stars for price, lack of key coverage, and quality of sticker cut. Some stickers weren't full cut or cut too much that the brown paper backing came with the sticker as I peeled it off. One tip when using - you might get some over hang when applied to smaller keys. I was able to apply the sticker centered, then use a sharp blade to trim it back. Just be careful not to gouge your keys.

review_text:
I have an iMac which came with the Apple compact wireless (bluetooth) keyboard. I like the way it works/types but it eats batteries pretty quickly and really why does a keyboard need to be wireless? It sits in the same spot all the time and is easily within reach of the computer to plug it in.

After the batteries died the 5th time I got this keyboard as a potential replacement. It works ok but unfortunately I really don't like it. I spend a lot of time at the keyboard and so am pretty picky about how they work.

My biggest complaint is that the overall height of the keyboard is much more than the low profile Apple keyboards, and the front edge is maybe 1/2" high. This requires me to hold my hands in a higher position and bend my wrists more which I find uncomfortable. I didn't realize how much I liked Apple's low-profile design until I tried this keyboard.

The "throw" of the keys is also much more, so it requires more action on each key, which I also don't like, and my fingers bump into the adjacent keys as I type which I don't like. Somehow about half the time I hit the return key twice in a row (like to end a paragraph) I actually type three returns, not sure why. I type pretty fast though, maybe just too fast for this keyboard :-).

The keyboard layout is different, the four keys at the bottom left "function", "control", "option" and "command" are all the same size which I don't like, most Apple keyboards have a larger command button because it's more often used.

The function keys are totally different, F1 does "close current window" which I find super annoying since if you hit it accidentally you lose your work in your current window. This happened once while I was typing this review in fact! The function keys are smaller so it's easier to hit the wrong one. Changing screen brightness requires the function key too which I don't like. The arrow keys are full sized which is a plus, but it affects the layout of all of the keys around it.

Overall I guess I did not realize how much I liked the Apple keyboards and will be sending this one back, and will try to find an Apple, wired, compact keyboard -- basically the same one I have now but wired.

review_text:
Well, I am glad that I have a way to watch my new HDX4 on my big HDTV again. I didn't buy last year's version due to the fact that there was no HDMI port to connect my Kindle to the TV. With the advent of the latest Kindle HDX 8.9" 4th generation, Amazon is offering a way to connect directly to the TV again. I went ahead and bought one of the new ones,(i.e. 4th generation only will this adapter work with) and was happy to find that it worked as advertised. My problem is that the adapter doesn't allow enough 'juice' through to the Kindle to charge properly while running. With my older HD 8.9", my 2.1A battery packs will charge the Kindle while running at a good rate. With this setup, it will charge with my new power charger,(at a VERY SLOOOOWWW rate) but not with any of my battery packs,(I have several different models and capacities up to 50000mAh all with charging ports of 2.1A). When I connect the HDX4 directly to the power charger, the charger,(the charger has six ports with a capacity of up to 2.4A per port) gets very warm and the Kindle charges very quickly! Using the power charger with a thicker longer cable will allow me to charge the HDX4 but very slowly while in use. Everything else I've tried loses ground while in use,(i.e. discharges).

All in all I am very happy to be able to once again directly connect my Kindles to the HDMI switch box I use for multiple devices. I can live with the currect slow recharge rate. It was just the learning curve that was required to find the correct combination of power source and cable to make it viable.
title: Great with a caveat...

review_text:
I’ve needed a bed tray for the longest time, but after several attempts to buy one that would work for me, I gave up. First of all, my body is too wide for most of them, and my belly is too big. The ones with the legs that fold down on either side never work out right for me and offer more aggravation than comfort. Then I have to find someplace to put it when I’m not using it.

When I saw this bed tray, I thought “What a great idea for fat people.” It’s made out of plastic. It comes flat with the pieces snapped in to the tray part, showing how to fold it up when you want to so pay attention to that. The instructions in English were the tiniest type I’ve ever seen, so forget about reading them. But you can figure it out. I’m probably not going to be breaking it down to stow it in a backpack or on a shelf, so it doesn’t matter to me—why? Because it’s so darned useful! I mean, really.

It’s not a one-trick pony, an item to help you be more comfortable with your tablet or laptop in bed. On the contrary! It works great to hold cookbooks in the kitchen; the little rubber-tipped prong things on the bottom foldout tray shelf do a great job of holding a hardbound cookbook by its front and back boards, keeping it stable on the countertop but allowing for flipping through the pages. A binder clip or rubber band can hold the pages open if the book doesn’t tend to want to lie flat. You can see those prongs holding my Kindle Fire in one of the photos.

The tray adjusts to different angles, including flat for use as a little table for eating in bed. Hey, when you’ve decided to spend the day in bed because you just don’t feel well enough to get out of it, it’s nice to have a place to put a plate. My favorite use for it, though, is turned so the longest part of the bottom lip is tucked up under my bed bolster and the edge of the tray is resting against the bolster. This provides a very stable, sturdy, little bed table that can hold a phone or tablet upright in the top slot (cables can go through the bottom if needed) and an Apple TV remote plus a drinking glass and a big bowl of popcorn.

Such a simple little thing, but so great. I love it!
title: This is not a one-trick pony

review_text:
Most people may assume that since this product ([[ASIN:B008195P34 Panasonic NiMH AAA Rechargeable Battery for Cordless Phones]]) bears the Panasonic brand name, it must be the best replacement batteries for Panasonic DECT 6.0 cordless phones. But that's not necessarily the case.

First, check the battery compartment of your Panasonic cordless phone (for example, the [[ASIN:B001P80ESO Panasonic KX-TG1062M DECT 6.0 Cordless/Corded Phone]]). If you see just two loose AAA cells instead of a battery pack, you're in luck! You can put any AAA rechargeable NiMH cells in there, and the phone won't know the difference. When the handset is placed into the charging cradle, the charger won't know the difference either. So it will just continue to charge the batteries at a low current (around 50mA). As long as your replacement batteries have capacity equal or higher than the original batteries, you are good to go.

That said, I highly recommend getting some good-quality LSD (Low-Self-Discharge, also known as 'Pre-Charged') rechargeable batteries, instead of either genuine Panasonic brand or off-brand rechargeable batteries. This is because:

1. The Panasonic NiMH AAA battery have capacities of 700mAh, which is very low by today's standard. Most rechargeable NiMH AAA cells on the market have capacity of 800mAh or higher.

2. Off-brand batteries advertise higher capacities such as '1000mAh', but they usually suffer from rapid self-discharge problem. That means if you leave the handset outside the cradle for just a few days, the batteries will be dead due to self-discharge.

3. LSD batteries are pre-charged from the factory, and they are ready to use right out of the package. That means you can start using your phone with those batteries right away. (Note that the phone may still insist the batteries need to be charged for 7 hours, simplest because it assumes any newly replaced batteries must be empty)

4. LSD batteries are rated for much longer lifespan (typically 1000 cycles) compared to ordinary NiMH batteries (typically 500 cycles).

As of this writing, you can get about 8 good-quality LSD cells for the same price as just 6 of those Panasonic batteries. Consider, for examples:
- [[ASIN:B004SB1TD4 Sanyo eneloop AAA Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries]] (800mAh)
- [[ASIN:B00CWNMW1S AmazonBasics AAA Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries]] (the white version is actually rebranded eneloop)
- [[ASIN:B003I2ZPFC GP ReCyko AAA Rechargeable Batteries Pre-Charged]] (850mAh)
- [[ASIN:B0040ZKD5I Tenergy Centura AAA Low Self-Discharge NiMH Rechargeable Batteries]] (rated 800mAh but measured ~900mAh)

All those batteries above offer higher capacities at lower prices compared to the original Panasonic batteries. Prices also vary depending on the package (4 or 8-pack) you pick, so shop around to get the best value. You can always use the remaining batteries in other household appliance.

[Side Note]
Panasonic purchased Sanyo a few years ago, so all 'Sanyo' brand batteries are manufactured by Panasonic now.
title: You don't have to use Panasonic rechargeable batteries for Panasonic phones

review_text:
I use door alarms in several locations inside my home and have for almost 10 years now.
Taking what I have learned from using similar products into account, as well as my experience with this set of seven, I see these particular door/window alarms as having very specific strengths and one limitation.

The best thing about these alarms, in my opinion, is that they run on widely available and very affordable AAA batteries, so you do not need to go looking for any expensive or difficult to find lithium batteries.
The other obvious pro is that you get a lot of alarms for a very reasonable price per alarm.
That is not only good if you want to alarm multiple doors,and windows, but also so you have back-ups because over time all the door alarms I have had eventually break down; particularly when they are on exterior doors/windows where they are exposed to heat, cold, and/or sun.

I will add that installing these on a door or window with a flush surface is about as easy as applying a sticker.
The added caveat about flush surfaces is included as a heads up to first time users of this style of door alarm.
If the door or window you want to use these alarms on is recessed, has molding, or any other design features that will not allow the two pieces of the alarm to be placed side by side, then you may need to improvise installation or look for a different type of alarm.

The main issue I have with these particular alarms is that they only offer an alarm function.
What I mean by that is many similar alarms include the option to choose between an alarm and a simple, much quieter, chime, which these do not.
That is fine if you wish to place them on a rarely used window or door for security purposes, but is a significant limitation if you want to place them on a door/window that you open and close frequently.
You can of course turn the alarm off, then back on each time you want to activate it, but I personally find that a bit annoying because the switch is small and I am one of those people who has a tendency to forget that sort of thing.

To sum up...
If you understand in advance what these alarms can and cannot do, they are an extremely affordable and convenient way to add a little extra security to many doors and windows.

Fire TV in itself is no big deal. If you’re already subscribed to HBO, Netflix, Hulu, etc. it’s only a convenience to have it pre-programmed into the TV. The only Fire TV I watched was imdbTV but it’s the same repeated shows for weeks and months at a time so now I hardly bother. If you’re an Amazon Prime member you can watch movies and shows on a per-view price of a couple of bucks. You can download other free movie/TV apps but I’m not very fond of reading privacy policies so I passed.

If you connect the TV to the internet and then disconnect it to use an air antenna alone, it no longer shows the channel/show information properly. A few times I would have to unplug the TV completely from the wall and replug it to even get a picture so the TV software has some bugs. Doing a full reset on the TV seems to have fixed both but I’ll only rarely ever plug it back in to the internet again except to see if there is a software update.

review_text:
In my house, where I have a giant antenna attached to my vintage stereo, this little gadget works passably if I find just the right spot in the room to set it. In my 1988 vintage car (with factory radio) it barely registers on the radio at all. I will qualify this with the additional information that here in Phoenix there is very little space on the FM dial that isn't already being used. Even so, I can get stations in my car from small towns many hours away but I can't get a clear signal from this little device from six inches away. My guess is that it simply doesn't broadcast strongly enough to overcome the electrical field in the vehicle.
Since it does function in the house I can't say it doesn't work, but I can't say it is worth buying, either. Fortunately, it was inexpensive enough that the experiment hasn't hurt which accounts for the higher two-star rating.
UPDATE: The company (LDream) monitors reviews of their products. After I posted this one they sent me an email offering a free replacement via coupon (I still had to pay shipping) on the assumption that the first one may be defective. That was nice. However, the replacement works exactly as well, or as poorly, as the first one. I was able to use it at work through a small boom box, but only if it was within four inches of the antenna. Within that four inches it was great. Still wasn't able to use it in the car. Oh, well.
BUT WAIT! The company waited a week, then called me on the phone to ask me how it went. The rep on the line had severely handicapped English speaking skills, but I was finally able to divine that the main reason for the call was to ask that I upgrade my review to at least three stars. I couldn't promise that, but I did attempt to give some constructive feedback should they want to improve the product. I might have considered it were I speaking with a person who understood what I was saying and didn't spend the majority of the call saying, "Um, ah, um, well, um" when trying to formulate any response. It was sad. Anyway, there you go, that's what happened. I'm giving both of these transmitters away on the off chance they might work better in a newer vehicle.
title: Snazzy But Useless

Reason I purchased this design (versus ALL the other ones that are designed like a cave, and stand open at all times) was because I'm 40 years old and had no desire to stick my hand in an obnoxiously puffy, colorful animal or doll head every 30 seconds. Why on earth can't I find one of these that doesn't look like it was made for a 5 year-old? Us old people get cold fingers too :(

Can someone please make more options for adults? My poor freezing fingers will thank you.

review_text:
Great little Class D amp capable of driving a set of Elac Uni-Fi UB5s much louder than I can reasonably listen to them in an apartment. I didn't want to find space for a large receiver or integrated amplifier at my desk, so I took a chance on this. The STMicro TDA7498E (not TI as listed in the description) chip amp looked to meet my requirements on power and THD. After reviewing its datasheet against the popular TI TPA3116, it appeared to me as the better component.

The aluminum channel enclosure is sleek and feels solid. It blends in nicely under a 27" monitor, and I appreciate the minimalism of a power switch and volume knob. I did not experience any sparking from the barrel plug. This issue appears to have been addressed with an inrush limiting circuit; on the bottom side of the board there is a TPCA8051 silkscreen designator corresponding to a FET that probably serves this purpose. Teardown photos are included. The PCBA appears to be quite well manufactured, and was clearly built on an automated line versus hand assembly. Nice to find at this price point.

However, here's my one gripe as an EE that is no stranger to questioning specifications. It's disingenuous to say that this amp could deliver 160W+160W RMS. That is indeed the nominal datasheet spec for the TDA7498E, but it's only achievable under the following conditions: Vcc=36V, RL=4 Ohm, and THD=10%. The power supply shipped with this unit is only 24V, and the internal electrolytic caps are only rated to 35V. Assuming we want to stick to <1% THD with our 24V power supply and stock caps, Figure 4 in the datasheet tells us that we're able to source 60W+60W RMS into a 4 Ohm load. For 0.1% THD this figure is reduced slightly. 60W per channel is very much loud enough for my application, but it may matter to you!

Overall, I'd recommend this unit.
title: Great unit, but not 160Wpc RMS in the real world

review_text:
I mainly wanted a newer digital watch, and this one fit my needs and provided additional life details I have been finding to be important. Main one is sleep tracking, which has some issues for me. Others may not be bothered by the data holes. I call it a data hole because I write software for lab instrumentation data access, and when data gets dropped.....that's a data hole to me.

In this case the Zepp app provides the kind of access I desire to monitor specific aspects of my health. I now mention Zepp because it's unclear as to which is at fault the watch or the app.

Example scenario of the problem, if I go to sleep, the watch and Zepp start tracking my sleep. When I wake up, it stops tracking my sleep. And therein lies the problem, when I wake it stops tracking my sleep. If I wake to go relieve myself, then get right back into bed, the watch and app occasionally keeps the record correctly, a blip in the data indicating I was most likely awake for a short bit. But most times it stops the record, then when I fall back asleep it starts all over, resetting or clearing out earlier data for the night. So, when I know I was in bed at 8pm or 10pm, wake up at 5am, up to relieve myself at 12:30, and the app shows I was asleep for 4hrs, that's a data problem.

Overall, I love the watch, just wish someone would fix this data issue regarding a wearers daily sleep. Even showing daily sleep as segments for the day would help.
title: Sleep Tracking Data Hole

review_text:
First let me state that I would not be considered an average user for this product. I am a computer professional with more than 30 years of experience, things that appears easy/obvious to me may not be so for everyone else. I am not better or smarter than anyone else, I just may have more experience. I also have much experience with Tivo. I was a DirecTV customer from 1996 until 2018 (cordcutting or is that satellite-cutting). When the DirecTV Tivo DVR was released I purchased one, very early adopter. The first thing I did was void the warranty and upgrade the hard drive. I've had as many as 4 units operational at the same time in my home. I lost track of how many failing hard drives I replaced, or upgraded for increased capacity for myself, family, or friends. Probably 60 or more. Chances are I will probably do so with this unit at some point. I purchased this unit because I wanted the major broadcast channels without paying an additional $60 a month for their streaming equivalents. I had Hulu, but NBC dropped out of the partnership, and I got most ABC content from Disney. Dropped Hulu as well since Disney only offers a commercials supported Hulu as a package, and must take ESPN (useless).

First setting up. There is a set top box, power supply, and LAN cable. Strangely the Tablo offers internaI SATA hard drive support and external USB hard drive support, but not an external eSATA connection. An internal drive generates a lot of heat, in addition to that of the actual Tablo electronics. USB though a slower option really is the only option at this point in the installation. Most likely I will extend the internal SATA connection at some point, right now I just want to get it running during the return window. I downloaded the Android and Roku apps, set up the unit which was straightforward. I got the 4 tuner unit because my experience with Tivo showed me that with a 2 tuner unit you miss a lot of recordings because of not enough tuners. I'll come back to this. The hard drive was formatted with no problems. When choosing a hard drive I chose a 3Tb NAS Western Digital drive. I think it will last longer. With multiple users it seemed the best choice, opinions may vary. About 700+ hours of HD recording time. Now the problems begin, scanning for channels. Never liked this on digital TVs. I can literally see the two major antenna sites from my home. Unfortunately digital TV instead of a signal strength Metter is scan and move, scan and move. Omni directional antennas are misleading, mostly it means it can move omnidirectionally, not receive omnidirectionally without moving the antenna. It took more than an hour to find a position that had sufficient strength on all the channels I desired. Again, I am only looking for 5 or 6 channels. Still haven't opened Getting Started, it is very straightforward, I cannot fault setting it up. However the first scheduled program failed because of a "weak signal". I could not view that channel, even though it was full bars green when I saved the channel list. Now it showed red. I rescanned without changing anything, again full bars green? Is this going to be a problem? Was this a single tuner, or the whole device?

I started adding programs to record, even stuff I know I will delete just to make the unit work as hard as possible. You will still get conflicts with a 4 tuner unit. Expect many more with a 2 tuner unit. Many, many more. This is where Tablo fails badly, very badly! Tivo had a master list of the programs you wished to record. You could move your must sees to the top of the list, the I don't cares, to the bottom. Tablo uses the date you selected the program to establish priority. If .Punky Brewster was the first program You picked, it will be recorded before the Super Bowl you chose a year later. Yes there is a conflict resolution screen where you can do a one time fix, but next time is Punky Brewster Time! Apparently this has been a long-time complaint.

So I am continuing to evaluate. The conflict resolution problem will only become more severe. The tuner problem I am not confident in at this point. I'll just have to keep checking daily.

Update 1:
Tuner stability continues to be a problem. Also Commercial Skip was permanently removed as of August 2022 and will no longer be offered to new purchasers! Not a deal breaker, but reducing features basically because of server cost makes me nervous regarding future support. The channel list does not have even the most basic of descriptions for the channels you receive. You have to Google the channel to find out what programming it carries. Again, not a deal breaker, but a sign the software is a work in progress.

Update 2: I checked the internal temperatures with an infrared thermometer, nominal temps are 105-110F. However, the area directly over the hard drive slot is 140-150+F. I suspect this is the reason for reports of premature hard drive failure. As such I would not recommend an internal hard drive. While working with the unit I found that scheduling information is contained within the Tablo not the hard drive. So if you change the hard drive you will lose your recordings, but not your schedule, which is a plus.

***************************************

I neither received nor solicited recompense in any form for this review. Solicitations to change or "enhance" reviews are always reported to Amazon without exception. Free items or money are joyfully accepted, THEN IMMEDIATELY REPORTED TO AMAZON!! THANK YOU!!!! The observations are my own without any outside influence or input. Your experience may differ from my own! Do your own research and comparisons prior to purchasing, don't rely solely on my observations. I recommend purchasing only from Prime sellers as my experience with "marketplace" sellers has been mostly negative, often drop shipping from China to the USA so it has a USA postmark. That said, do your own research prior to purchasing any products from the Internet!?
